paper_metadata.title: The Effects of Grain Size and Carbon Content on the Ductility of Recrystallized Molybdenum Wire
paper_metadata.journal: Transactions of the Japan Institute of Metals

evidence.section: III.5 The effect of carbon content on the ductility
evidence.quote: this shows that the low ductility in the low carbon specimen is attributable to the low cohesion of grain boundaries, and that carbon increases the grain boundary cohesion.

evidence.section: III.5 The effect of carbon content on the ductility
evidence.quote: In the range of dT-1/2<5mm-1/2 (dT>0.04mm), carbon suppresses the intergranular brittleness and increases the ductility.

mechanisms.name: cleavage fracture promotion by coarse carbides

evidence.section: III.5 The effect of carbon content on the ductility
evidence.quote: An excess amount of carbon yields coarse carbides and promotes cleavage fracture, thus decreasing the ductility(9)(10).

The fundamental mechanism of fracture can be considered as the stress concentration by the pile-up of dislocations regardless of whether the fracture initiation is at a grain boundary or in a matrix(33)(34).

The ductile-brittle transition with the change of dT, therefore, may be explained qualitatively by Cottrell's theory(23), which predicts that the fracture changes from ductile to brittle cleavage with increasing grain size under a proper testing condition.

Low carbon specimens (C≦10ppm) were extremely low in ductility due to an intergranular brittleness when the average grain diameter in the transverse cross section of the specimen (dT) was larger than about 0.04mm
Thus, these specimens can essentially be classified into low (specimens A and B), medium (specimen C) and high (specimen D) carbon specimens.

In high carbon specimens (C=210 ppm) the ductility increased nearly linearly with increasing dT-1/2.
